headline: Ukraine’s Deep Strikes Grow in Scale and Scope Across Russia and Beyond

paragraphs.text: Forty Russian oil and military-industrial sites struck in 50 days, including a fuel terminal on the Arctic White Sea and a missile-propellant plant deep in Siberia. A Russian military cargo ship set ablaze in the Baltic Sea. A warship sunk off the coast of Libya. And, in a flash of fire, a section of roadway on Russia’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea sent crashing into the sea.

Ukraine has been accelerating a deep-strike campaign that now stretches more than 1,500 miles and spans at least five seas, aiming to sever the networks that keep Moscow’s war machine fueled, armed and financed. In doing so, Kyiv is turning Russia’s immense geographic scale and far-flung military and economic assets into a liability.

Russia still holds a clear advantage in long-range strike abilities. Moscow can target any corner of Ukraine with ballistic missiles that Kyiv is largely defenseless against without more U.S.-made interceptors. With its superior troop numbers and weaponry, Russia is calculating that it can outlast Ukraine. Moscow is trying to inflict pain on Ukrainian civilians and push Kyiv closer to surrender by attacking power plants, heating grids and rail infrastructure heading into winter.
But Ukraine has its own cards to play. Ukrainian forces are increasing the tempo of their long-range operations to record levels, firing more than 1,000 drones into Russia on some days.

Kyiv has continued hitting Russian refineries, sending production to a two-decade low, despite President Trump’s demand to stop. Ukraine has conducted audacious long-range attacks even after Elbridge Colby, the U.S. under secretary of defense, scolded Kyiv this month over “the spectacle of deep strikes,” saying they “have not been effective in driving an end to the war.”

Kyrylo Budanov, the head of presidential office in Ukraine, has acknowledged that “long-range strikes alone will not win the war.” But he has argued that every hit “means repairs, lost production, logistics reorganization and additional costs,” making it harder for Russia to sustain the fighting.
The attacks also force Moscow to redeploy air-defense systems away from the front line and move naval assets to protect vessels at sea.
Both sides’ campaigns are spilling well beyond the borders of their enemy.

Moscow is waging a shadow war of arson, sabotage and assassination plots across Europe, alongside incursions in NATO airspace and attacks on ships in the territorial waters of NATO nations. Kyiv, for its part, is hunting far and wide for Russian military assets in an effort to undermine Moscow’s ability to project power.
The breadth of Ukraine’s campaign was driven home this past week when Ukrainian drones struck a Russian military cargo ship, the Sparta II, in the Gulf of Finland in the eastern Baltic Sea.

The next morning, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine, seven naval drones tore through defensive fire in the Libyan port of Benghazi. The swarm sank the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, along with an onboard combat helicopter, and struck a Russian cargo ship that the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said was hauling weapons.

Officials in the government that controls eastern Libya vowed to retaliate. Mr. Zelensky has defended strikes on Russian targets anywhere in the world as a sovereign right to self-defense, calling them “our long-term security guarantee.”

While Ukraine’s European allies have defended strikes inside Russia, the initial reaction to Ukrainian strikes in the Baltic and Mediterranean Seas has been more cautious, said Aliona Hlivko, the head of St. James’s Foreign Policy Group, a research organization in London.

Some fear that Russia could view such attacks as an escalation, she said, a contention that Mr. Colby, the U.S. defense official, also made. After Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy said that the war “should not and cannot be extended to the Mediterranean,” Mr. Zelensky said he called Ms. Meloni and confirmed that the attack “was conducted without prior coordination with our European partners.”

Others, acknowledging that Europe has “no credible response” to Russia’s shadow war, Ms. Hlivko said, are more supportive of the strikes, as Ukraine offers the only real direct pushback against Moscow. Kyiv, Ukrainian analysts said, is filling a vacuum left by Europe’s fear of direct confrontation with Russia and by the Trump administration’s embrace of Moscow.
“Europe is our rear guard, and we are its army,” Andrii Klymenko, the head of the Black Sea Institute of Strategic Studies, said of Ukraine.
The question of whether Ukraine’s strategy can compel Russia to engage in serious negotiations has highlighted a stark policy rift between the United States and Europe.

After Mr. Colby criticized Ukraine’s long-range campaign during NATO talks in Brussels, European defense chiefs offered retorts. The German defense minister, Boris Pistorius, called Mr. Colby’s remarks “quite a stupid thing.” The British defense secretary, Wes Streeting, said of Ukraine’s campaign, “There’s no doubt in my mind that it is buying time and saving lives.”
Independent analysts have largely aligned with the European perspective.

“Continuing to resource Ukraine’s deep strikes is critical to bringing Russia to negotiations, rather than the Potemkin talks currently being orchestrated by Washington,” Jack Watling, a military expert at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, wrote this past week.

As the Trump administration has tried to jump-start negotiations to end the war by offering incentives to Moscow, Ukraine has unleashed some of its largest assaults of the war. On Nov. 16, the Russian military reported downing 1,336 Ukrainian drones, breaking a record set 18 days before. On Nov. 17, the record fell again, with 1,441 reported interceptions.

Moscow does not say how many Ukrainian drones get through, and it rarely acknowledges damage caused by the attacks. But military analysts using geo-located video footage have verified dozens of significant strikes in recent weeks.

Mr. Putin publicly remarked on Tuesday that Russia’s domestic petroleum market remained difficult and complained that Ukraine had not heeded the Trump administration’s warnings against hitting Russian refineries.

Ukraine is targeting every link in the refinery chain, from upstream pipeline blending and pumping stations to primary refining plants, petrochemical processing facilities and maritime export outlets.

Russian refinery output is roughly 30 percent below the level of a year earlier, according to the International Energy Agency. With gasoline production down 20 percent and diesel down nearly 30 percent, Moscow has restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies.
Ukraine is also targeting the networks that enable Russian missile strikes, including plants critical to weapons production, and the planes and ground launchers used in assaults.

Kyiv’s expanding reach is powered by the rapid growth of its domestic defense industry. Those capabilities have evolved from retrofitting commercial drones to building jet-powered strike systems and heavy cruise missiles capable of carrying a one-ton payload more than 1,800 miles. Ukraine is also racing to produce its own ballistic missiles.

At the same time, Ukrainian engineers are rapidly integrating artificial intelligence across the country’s arsenal. “Hundreds of Ukrainian defense tech companies are already using A.I.,” Mr. Zelensky said on Tuesday.

The increase in domestic output has been paired with joint production agreements with Germany for reconnaissance drones and with Britain to build more than 1,000 long-range strike drones. The push is intended to sustain Ukraine’s deep-strike capacity regardless of political shifts in Washington.
